system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2135-12-13 12:16:00 to 2135-12-14 13:00:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A male patient with a history of type 1 diabetes, end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis, chronic diastolic heart failure, seizure disorder, and known esophagitis was admitted for epigastric pain, nausea, vomiting, and a persistent dry cough. His symptoms were consistent with a flare of his chronic esophagitis, and he reported improvement after receiving standard care. He underwent his scheduled hemodialysis during the admission, which contributed to symptom resolution. His cough was attributed to post-nasal drip, with a normal chest X-ray and no signs of infection. The patient was managed with an increase in pantoprazole to twice daily, as previously recommended by gastroenterology, and a cough suppressant for nighttime symptoms. He remained stable throughout the stay, tolerated a regular diet, and was discharged home in stable condition with instructions to continue his home medications and follow up with his specialists.

INDICATION:  ___ male with recent gastric biopsy and now with fever
and myalgias.  Evaluate lungs and look for evidence of free air or
perforation.

COMPARISON:  Multiple studies including most recent of ___ and ___.

SINGLE UPRIGHT AP VIEW OF THE CHEST:  The lungs are clear without focal
consolidation, pneumothorax or pleural effusion.  There is no free air beneath
the diaphragm.  The heart size and pulmonary vasculature are similar compared
to the prior exam.  Hilar contours are normal.

IMPRESSION:  
1.  No free air beneath the diaphragm.

2.  Stable cardiomegaly without evidence of volume overload.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. ___ . I'm Dr. ___ , one of the hospitalists. I understand you came in today from transplant clinic feeling unwell. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve had a fever, body aches, and I’ve been dizzy. Also had some diarrhea a few times yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. How high did the fever feel? And did you measure it at all?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: They said it was 101.7 in the ER. It’s been coming and going.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s mild but enough to make you feel lousy. Any cough, sore throat, or shortness of breath?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just a little dry cough, nothing bad. No chest pain this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. I see you’re on hemodialysis. Did you get your treatment this week?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I was supposed to go tomorrow, but I came here instead because I felt so bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Understood. We’ll make sure you get dialysis tomorrow. That might help you feel better, especially since you’re not urinating much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I’ve been swollen a bit in my legs too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep an eye on that. You had a chest X-ray and EKG done shortly after arrival. The X-ray showed your lungs are clear—no pneumonia or fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I was worried it might be an infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We sent a flu test and blood cultures just to be safe. You said you got your flu shot this year?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, at the transplant clinic last month.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s helpful. It doesn’t rule out a virus completely, but it lowers the risk of severe flu. Your EKG was stable—no new heart issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had heart problems before, so I get nervous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’re monitoring everything. Your blood pressure was a bit high earlier—185 over 92—but it’s come down with fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It usually runs high. I take meds for it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and we’ll continue those. We also gave you a liter of saline to help with dehydration from the fever and diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do feel a bit better since the IV.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to hear. Now, I see from your records that you had an endoscopy recently. Did they find anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, they said there were some sores in my stomach and esophagus. Mild gastritis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right. Erosions in the lower esophagus and stomach lining. That can cause discomfort, but it’s not severe. We’ll keep you on your usual acid-reducing medication.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m on pantoprazole twice a day now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s correct. We’ll continue that. No signs of bleeding or perforation on the X-ray, so that’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I was worried about that after the biopsy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Completely understandable. But everything looks stable. For now, we’re treating this as a mild viral infection—likely an upper respiratory virus—given your fever, aches, and cough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not the flu?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The rapid test came back negative, so it’s not influenza. But other viruses can cause similar symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. Antibiotics don’t work for viruses. We’ll wait for the blood cultures, but if they’re negative, we’ll stick with supportive care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You look better today. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. Fever’s gone, and I haven’t had diarrhea since yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Your blood cultures came back negative—no infection in the bloodstream. So we’re confident this was a viral illness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’ll get your scheduled hemodialysis today, and after that, we’ll discharge you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need any new meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. Just continue your home medications—insulin, blood pressure pills, pantoprazole, and your dialysis schedule.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if the fever comes back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your transplant team or come back to the ER. But I don’t expect it to. You’ve turned the corner.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I was really worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Rest up after dialysis, stay hydrated, and follow up with your specialists as planned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check-in before discharge. You completed hemodialysis and are doing well. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’m good. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in clinic if needed.

summary.summary_paragraph: A male patient with a history of type 1 diabetes, end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis, chronic systolic heart failure, seizure disorder, and esophageal reflux was admitted from transplant clinic with a one-day history of fever, myalgias, dizziness, and diarrhea. Initial evaluation revealed a low-grade fever and stable vital signs after IV fluids. Chest X-ray showed clear lungs and no free air, and EKG was unchanged. Rapid flu testing was negative, and blood cultures showed no growth. His symptoms were attributed to a mild viral upper respiratory infection. He received supportive care, including hydration and antipyretics, and completed his scheduled hemodialysis. He improved rapidly, afebrile by the morning of discharge, and was discharged home in stable condition with instructions to continue his home medications and follow up with his specialists.
